stories.headline: Update: UK and EU Reach Set of Deals to Deepen Post-Brexit Relationship
stories.summary:
The United Kingdom and the European Union have reached a set of agreements aimed at deepening their post-Brexit relationship, Bloomberg reported on Friday. The deals come as China, the United States and Russia are reshaping the global order, a backdrop that has pushed London and Brussels toward closer cooperation.

The agreements follow earlier reporting that the two sides were preparing to agree a youth mobility scheme for up to 100,000 people a year. Today's development is that a broader package of deals has now been concluded, extending beyond the mobility arrangement already covered.

The agreements represent a further step in the gradual reset of ties since the UK left the bloc. Supporters on both sides argue that closer coordination is needed amid geopolitical uncertainty, while critics in the UK have long warned that deeper alignment with Brussels risks undercutting the purpose of Brexit. Detailed terms of the package were not fully available in the initial report.

Further details on the scope of the deals, and any steps needed for ratification by the UK Parliament and EU member states, are expected to emerge in the coming days.

stories.headline: Update: Army Delays Iowa Lead Azide Detonation to Monday Amid Lawsuit
stories.summary:
The US Army has postponed its planned detonation of five tonnes of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, from Friday to Monday. Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced the delay Thursday evening on X, saying public safety is the Army's top priority and that Monday is the latest possible moment before a forecast temperature drop that could further destabilize the material.

Environmental groups sued Thursday to stop the detonations, arguing the Army failed to consider safer alternatives or give adequate notice. The Army says the operation is a planned, controlled safety measure permitted by the Environmental Protection Agency, which granted an emergency permit for 68 drums of the material, citing an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment.

The Army warns that two rapid detonations could send a plume of lead-containing dust over eastern Iowa and into Illinois, with contaminants potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces. Blasts could also damage buildings and shatter windows nearby. Residents of Middletown, a community of about 360 people, have been asked to leave for roughly six hours, from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. local time, and all people are urged to avoid outdoor activity in affected areas.

The lead azide, a volatile detonator compound, has been stored for more than 20 years in earth-covered underground tanks in a bath of ethanol and water. A routine check this year found some water had evaporated, leaving the material too unstable to move safely, officials said.

stories.headline: Senate Budget Chairman Johnson Calls Social Security a 'Legal Ponzi Scheme' in New Report
stories.summary:
Senate Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson, a Wisconsin Republican, has released a report titled "Social Security: The Reality... a Legal Ponzi Scheme," first obtained by Fox News Digital. Johnson argues Americans have been misled about how the program works and that it cannot be fixed once it begins to collapse.

The report projects that Social Security will become insolvent by 2032, producing a shortfall of roughly $511 billion, about 21 percent of a projected $2.4 trillion federal deficit that year. Johnson contends that payroll taxes are not held in a "lock box" but are used immediately to pay current beneficiaries or fund other government programs, and that future benefits will rely on taxes from today's workers plus borrowing. He blames past decisions by Congress, including not investing surpluses and promising increasingly expensive benefits.

The framing is likely to draw sharp responses. Supporters of the program, including most Democrats, have long argued that Social Security is an earned, insured benefit funded by dedicated payroll contributions, and that insolvency can be addressed through adjustments to revenue or benefits, with trust fund reserves allowing continued partial payment. Johnson, who has said he will chair the committee for about two more months, and other fiscal conservatives argue the program's finances demand urgent structural change.

stories.headline: South Africa Reports 581 Women Killed in Three Months
stories.summary:
South Africa's latest crime statistics, released Friday, show 581 women were killed between July and September, including 131 in Gauteng province, which contains Johannesburg. Police recorded 5,590 murders overall, 204 fewer than in the same period last year, though that still averages about 60 killings a day.

It is unclear whether the figure for women represents an increase or decrease, because police had recently stopped publishing such numbers, citing significant anomalies in the data. The period included the discovery of 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg, a series that triggered national outrage.

Gauteng's police chief, General Tommy Mthombeni, said Thursday that eight people have been arrested in connection with those 13 killings, including three over the death of runner Elizabeth Moselakgomo. Separately, five women and a toddler were shot dead in Botshabelo, Free State, on Wednesday night when three masked men opened fire on a family; no arrests have been made. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia called for greater efforts to prevent violence against women and children.

stories.headline: Update: Kushner Says Russia 'Comfortable' With NATO-Like Security Guarantees for Ukraine After Trump-Xi-Putin Summit
stories.summary:
U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine, following President Donald Trump's meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Kushner also said Trump is open to offering such guarantees to Kyiv. The remarks are the first concrete signal on the security architecture a settlement might include.

The guarantees are modeled on NATO's Article 5, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all. Analysts cited in coverage said that extending anything resembling that commitment to Ukraine "stretches credulity," given Moscow's long-standing opposition to Ukraine's alignment with the alliance and the political difficulty Washington would face in making such a pledge.

The statement follows the unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzhen, which we reported previously. Neither the Kremlin nor Kyiv had publicly confirmed Kushner's characterization in the coverage available. Supporters of a negotiated settlement see the comments as progress toward ending the war, while skeptics question whether Moscow's stated comfort would survive detailed terms, and whether Washington would commit forces or only political assurances.

What the guarantees would require, who would enforce them, and how Ukraine and European allies respond are the central open questions. Further talks are expected, and any formal proposal would draw scrutiny in Congress and among U.S. allies.

stories.headline: UK and EU Set to Agree Youth Mobility Scheme for Up to 100,000 People a Year
stories.summary:
The UK and European Union are expected to agree a youth mobility scheme at a summit in Brussels on Friday, the BBC understands. Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK each year, with the same number of young Britons allowed into Europe. Downing Street has not commented on the details but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.

The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators seek agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing. The government argues a food deal could remove checks and paperwork for exporters, add 5 billion pounds to the economy and cut food prices. Sticking points include the UK's request to cap numbers and the EU's demand that EU students pay the same tuition fees as domestic students.

Andy Burnham, speaking Thursday, said he would always be prepared to walk away but that lower food prices, reduced business costs and closer cooperation on immigration were too valuable to ignore. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused him of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum. Labour rejected a similar EU proposal in 2024, arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement, and now favors a time-limited, capped scheme with a ban on claiming benefits.

If a deal is secured, the government says it will introduce legislation in Parliament next week to implement the changes.

stories.headline: Houthi Forces Besiege Yemeni City of Taiz, Cutting Off Up to a Million People
stories.summary:
Houthi rebels fully encircled the government-controlled Yemeni city of Taiz last month, cutting off a population estimated at between 600,000 and 1 million people, according to BBC reporting from residents inside. Seven people interviewed described sharply limited food entering the city, with prices of rice, sugar and cooking oil doubling or tripling, and dwindling supplies of medicine, water and fuel.

Schools and restaurants are closed, and rebel snipers on surrounding hills make even short trips dangerous. The local Office for Siege Affairs says 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August, though estimates vary widely. Some residents declined to be named, fearing reprisals, and said the Houthis control key mobile carriers.

Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, is the gateway to Aden, the temporary seat of the internationally recognized government, and to southern Yemen. Iran-backed Houthi forces reached its outskirts in 2015 and have held the capital, Sanaa, since 2014. Saudi-backed forces are reportedly moving troops to protect Aden as the Houthis gain ground, a shift the BBC's security correspondent says could have dangerous consequences amid the wider regional confrontation involving Iran.

stories.headline: Texas Execution Takes Over an Hour as Staff Struggle to Find Veins
stories.summary:
Texas inmate Reinaldo Dennes was executed Thursday in Huntsville after a procedure lasting 63 minutes, as prison staff struggled to establish intravenous access. Dennes, convicted of capital murder in the 1996 killing of Houston diamond dealer Janos Szucs, was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. He repeatedly cried out during the procedure, according to witnesses cited by the Associated Press, saying "The pain! Go! Go!" and "My right leg is killing me!"

Texas Department of Criminal Justice spokesperson Amanda Hernandez said all procedures were followed and that staff made multiple unsuccessful attempts before placing needles in his left foot and the left side of his neck, locations she said comply with state procedures. She did not know how many attempts failed and suggested Dennes may have exaggerated his discomfort, noting he complained before the drugs flowed and in areas with no IV. "There was nothing abnormal on our part," she said.

The execution comes amid renewed scrutiny of lethal injection after a failed attempt in Tennessee in September, in which Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital that her attorneys said did not properly enter her bloodstream. Death penalty opponents say such cases show the method is unreliable, while supporters of capital punishment point to the state's assertion that protocols were followed and to the severity of the underlying crime.
